stemMd:
The laboratory notebooks of the nineteenth-century chemist Adèle Rousseau—thirty-one volumes, most of them written in a private shorthand that no one could read until a retired telegraph operator worked out its ______ are now held in the archive of the Musée Ferrand in Lyon.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanationMd:
Find the backbone of the sentence before you think about the blank. The subject is *The laboratory notebooks of the nineteenth-century chemist Adèle Rousseau* and the verb is *are now held*. Everything between them is a supplementary description of the notebooks, and it was opened with a dash after *Rousseau*.

A supplementary element must be closed with the same mark that opened it. An element opened with a dash is closed with a dash, so the blank needs **system—**.

What makes this hard is the comma after *volumes* inside the interruption. It invites the reader to treat the interruption as comma-bounded and to close it with a comma. But that comma belongs to the inside of the element: it separates *thirty-one volumes* from the phrase *most of them written in a private shorthand...*. Check by lifting the dashed element out entirely: "The laboratory notebooks of the nineteenth-century chemist Adèle Rousseau are now held in the archive of the Musée Ferrand in Lyon." The sentence stands, which confirms that the element runs from one dash to a second one.

distractorRationale.d: This closes with a comma an element that was opened with a dash. Mixed marks leave the dash unpaired, so the reader cannot tell where the interruption ends. The comma after 'volumes' makes this tempting, but that comma is inside the element.
distractorRationale.c: A semicolon separates two independent clauses. Here it would cut the subject off from its verb 'are now held', leaving neither side a complete sentence.
distractorRationale.a: With no punctuation, the dashed element is never closed, and the verb 'are now held' runs on as though it belonged to the clause about the telegraph operator.

accessibilityText: A sentence about the laboratory notebooks of the chemist Adèle Rousseau. After her name, a dash opens a description: thirty-one volumes, comma, most of them written in a private shorthand that no one could read until a retired telegraph operator worked out its, then a blank after which the sentence continues 'are now held in the archive of the Musée Ferrand in Lyon.' Each choice is the word system followed by different punctuation: the four choices are no punctuation, a dash, a semicolon, and a comma.

provenance.notes: Original item. Adèle Rousseau, her notebooks, the telegraph operator and the Musée Ferrand are invented; no source text was adapted.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The interruption opens with an em dash after 'Rousseau', so a matching dash must close it before 'are now held'. That gives B. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The interruption opens with an em dash after 'Rousseau', so it must close with a matching dash before the main verb 'are now held'. No punctuation, a semicolon or a comma all fail to close the dash pair, and a semicolon also splits the subject from its verb.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: Subject 'The laboratory notebooks of ... Adèle Rousseau', verb 'are now held'. The supplementary element opened by the dash after 'Rousseau' must be closed by a dash after 'system'. (The blank ends on a word rather than a year so that the choices are not read as numbers by the option-order and equivalence tools.) Comma mismatches the opening mark (the internal comma after 'volumes' is the lure); semicolon splits subject from verb; no punctuation never closes the element. Re-solved from the stem alone: same answer. Unique. Hard because the interrupting element is about twenty-five words long and contains its own comma, so the opening dash is far behind the reader when the blank arrives. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
